The 2026-08-05 ORA-wide once/day cadence policy collapsed it from `*/30 * * * *` to `0 11 * * *`, which destroyed its entire reason to exist — same-day drift detection *faster* than the daily guard. Its own v1.1 note recorded this ("Flagged as a retirement candidate, not retired").

**Producer-orphan check (register-scheduled-task v2.6 / setup-review C5) — PASSED.** Grepped `maintenance/`, `hooks/` and every live task SKILL.md for scripts this task was the sole invoker of. `repo_first_check.py` retains two live invokers: the `ora-skills` pre-commit hook (`--check-staged`) and `ora-doctrine-integrity-guard`'s daily engine 4 (verified at that task's `SKILL.md:20`, same absolute command). No script was orphaned — the failure mode that froze the dead-man chain for a week after `ora-setup-audit`'s 2026-06-16 retirement does not recur here.

**Coverage delta, accepted and recorded:** drift detection reverts from ~24h (the retired task's post-08-05 cadence) to the daily guard's 12:55 sweep — effectively no loss, since both were daily. What IS lost: the retired task additionally filed a durable OI-NNN item on findings; the daily guard alarms via email + Notion only. OI-075 amended to reflect this rather than closed.

**Ordering was INVERTED from the skill's default archive-first rule, deliberately and with proof.** `register-scheduled-task` mandates archive-then-delete because Cowork's sidebar delete is folder-destructive. That hazard does not apply to the CC MCP path: `delete_scheduled_task`'s own contract is registry-only ("Its SKILL.md file was left in place"). Meanwhile the opposite hazard does apply — `ora-task-integrity-guard`'s `guard.ps1:157` enumerates every registry entry on `id + filePath` with **no `enabled` filter** (read and verified this pass, not taken from the prior session's note), so archiving the folder while the entry lived would have made the guard resurrect it and report a restore every day. Actual sequence used, which satisfies both constraints: (1) `cp -r` the folder to `_archive_2026-08-09_retired/` and verify byte-identical — nothing destructive happens before a verified copy exists; (2) `delete_scheduled_task`; (3) confirm absence via `fleet-status.py`; (4) remove the original; (5) move the now-stale `_scheduled_tasks_backup/` copy into the same archive as `..__guard-backup`.

**Acceptance test.** Ran `guard.ps1` directly after removal: `{"checked":59,"restored":[],"missing_everywhere":[],"errors":[],"id_collisions":[]}` — no resurrection, no alarm, which is the specific outcome the inverted ordering was designed to produce.

**Also corrected in passing:** `session-context.md`'s scheduler-doctrine bullet ended with "Disabled tasks can't be folder-archived (the guard restores them) — remove via the Cowork UI first." That is LAMS-only guidance pointing at the folder-destructive control, and it is wrong for CC/MCP. Replaced with the per-fleet ordering proven above. Added a `⛔ Do NOT re-register` bullet naming this task id — the consolidated-checkable-place requirement that exists because retirements recorded only in a task's own frontmatter got resurrected during the 2026-07-08 recovery.

**Not done, flagged:** no LAMS twin existed (verified — `Documents\Claude\Scheduled\ora-skill-cache-drift-alert` absent), so no cross-fleet shared-file risk applied.

## 2026-08-09 — session-context line 18 de-dated; retired-task-roster pointer found DANGLING (rollover casualty), plus a correction to the entry above

Gabriel-directed continuation of today's tombstone consolidation, covering the three dates that had not yet crossed the 30-day WARN line (`2026-07-12`, `2026-07-16`, `2026-07-24` — due 2026-08-11, 08-15 and 08-23). Pre-emptive, so the fix lands once rather than three times.

**The real finding is not the dates — one of the pointers no longer resolved.** Line 18 read "Retired-task roster: `event_log.md`'s 2026-07-12 entry." No `## 2026-07-12` header exists in the live log. The 2026-07-16 rollover (`3083 → 604` lines) cut everything at or before its boundary into `memory/_archive/event_log_2026-07-16.md`, taking two same-day entries with it: "Session-context consolidation: integrity-guard + scheduled-task retirement history archived" (archive line 1075 — the roster this pointer wanted) and "Session-context consolidation: 2026-07-05/08 CC/MCP fleet-loss recovery archived" (archive line 1126). Anyone following the live-log citation would have found nothing and concluded the roster was lost. The rollover was a clean mechanical cut that altered no content; what it could not do is rewrite the inbound citations pointing INTO the range it moved. That is the durable lesson — **a log rollover silently breaks every dated cross-reference aimed at the cut range**, and session-context.md is the file most likely to hold them.

**Correction to the entry immediately above this one.** That entry stated the 2026-07-05 fleet-loss incident was "already archived to this log's 2026-07-12 consolidation entry." Wrong on location for the same reason: it is in `memory/_archive/event_log_2026-07-16.md`, not the live log. The substance stands — the incident IS archived and line 9 was correctly dropped as a pointer to a pointer — only the path was stale. Both entries now cite the archive.

**Retired from line 18, all three dates.** The retired-task roster anchor (2026-07-12), the retiming history anchor (2026-07-24 — this one does still resolve, at the "07:00 fleet collision cleared: ora-task-integrity-guard retimed 07:00 → 07:05 ET" entry in the live log), and "LAMS retired 2026-07-16" for ora-am-brief (resolves to the live "RATIFIED: LAMS ora-am-brief retired (migrated to CC/MCP)" entry, with the closed project file archived alongside it).

## 2026-08-09 — Claim-holder "phantom sessions" root-caused to two disjoint session-id namespaces; claim_work.py fixed (OI-108); guard pause lifted after the mtime fix landed (OI-107 CLOSED)

Follow-on from the same-day guard handoff relay. Three threads, all closed.

**1. The "untraceable" claim sessions were never untraceable — I looked them up in the wrong store.** Earlier in this session I reported that claim-holders `1d24d6a4` and `b09003a0` "don't resolve to anything in `list_sessions`" and framed it as a gap in the single-writer protocol. The miss was real; the conclusion was wrong. Root cause: a session carries TWO ids in disjoint namespaces — `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` (the agent id, e.g. `21c98da5-…`, used by claim files, the `session-state.d` fleet mirror's `_sid`, `session_liveness.py`, override tokens, both pre-push gates, `allocate-oi-id.py`) and `CLAUDE_CODE_HOST_SESSION_ID` (`local_<uuid>`, the ONLY id `list_sessions`/`send_message` accept). They cannot match. Verified both directions: every claim id checked resolves to a live record under `obsidian-fleet-mirror/session-state.d/`, and `local_*` ids appear in NO machine-written artifact under `~/.claude` — only in hand-written prose. Durable writeup: `reference_agent_vs_host_session_id_namespaces.md`.

**2. `claim_work.py` fixed and merged (OI-108, CLOSED).** Two defects. (a) Claims recorded only the agent id, so a colliding claim could be READ but its owner could not be CONTACTED. Fixed ADDITIVELY — `host_session_id` recorded alongside the agent id, which stays the ownership identity for renew/release/collision so claims remain joinable to the agent-id-keyed mirror; new `_clean_host_session_id()` normalizes at ONE reader choke point (non-string / blank / >128 chars / any char outside 0x21–0x7e all degrade to `""`); `renew_claim()` carries it forward; `list` and the SessionStart broadcast print `(message it at <host id>)`, sanitized. Fails open to `""`, deliberately not `"unknown"` (a legal agent id that would read as a real target). (b) `--paths` used bare `nargs="*"`, so a repeated flag silently kept only the LAST value — found live when a two-path claim covered one path, dropping the file being edited. Now `action="extend"`. No new imports: a plain character scan, not `re`, because the module is imported by `shared-checkout-guard.py` on every Edit/Write and its header documents that hot-path rule.

Merged to `main` as `8fca11d` (branch commit `369c62b`). Evidence: full `hooks/tests` **44/44 on main post-merge, 0 failures**; `test-claim-work-lib` 85/85 (was 55), `test-active-work-broadcast` 42/42 (was 23).

**Independent review, `claude-fable-5`, 2 rounds — round 1 was NOT a rubber stamp.** It returned CHANGES REQUIRED with 2 Important + 3 Minor. Both Importants were real: the first fix tested raw truthiness before sanitizing, and `_sanitize_field("")` returns `"(no description)"`, so whitespace/control-only host ids still rendered `(message it at (no description))` — the SECOND time that exact class slipped through in one change; and the renew test was tautological (renewed with the same host id already in the file, so it could not catch an env-re-read regression on the live `_self_renew_claims` path that fires on every Edit/Write). Round 2 APPROVED WITH NITS, with the reviewer mutation-testing both fixes to confirm the new tests BIND (gutted normalizer → 9+7 failures; renew re-reads env → exactly the 2 new assertions). Accepted residual, not fixed: no `local_<uuid>` shape check — strictly less expressive than the adjacent, already-unsanitized `description` field, and hard-coding a format observed once would risk silently rejecting a legitimate future target, i.e. re-creating the bug being closed.

**Process note:** recording the review verdict required an `allow-config-write` token (the gate matcher reads any write-shaped command naming `hooks/**`). Rather than reword the command to slip the matcher — guard evasion, and a defect class this setup has already hardened against twice — it was surfaced to Gabriel, who approved in-turn. Token was deleted immediately after the single recording write (0 remaining), rather than left to age out its 60-minute multi-use window.

**3. OI-107 CLOSED — the guard pause is lifted because its cause is gone.** The canonical-is-authoritative engine landed on `main` (`1af60c3`, hardened by `2e29fa7` after independent review + adversarial REFUTE) with `maintenance/task-integrity-lib.ps1`; `guard.ps1` now contains ZERO `LastWriteTime` references — mtime is out of the decision path entirely. Both `ora-task-integrity-guard` and `ora-health-guard` are enabled again with live next-run times, verified via `list_scheduled_tasks`. **Caution recorded for the next reader:** seeing both guards re-enabled after a Gabriel-directed pause LOOKS like a violated pause, and was nearly reported as one — the fix landing is what made re-enabling correct. Check whether the underlying cause is gone before escalating a re-enable. OI-107's `Auto-check` fired correctly and is what surfaced the closure at all; worth reusing for time-boxed pauses.

**All four 2026-08-09 model retags survived the entire episode intact** (`ora-skill-cache-drift-alert`, `ora-cc-schematic-refresh`, `ora-am-brief`, `ora-lease-snapshot-refresh` — all still `checked 2026-08-09`). No write was lost.

## 2026-08-09 — Why ora-skill-store-drift-check stopped posting: most likely a fleet-wide phantom-dispatch casualty, not independently confirmed for this task

Follow-up to the two entries above. Investigated why the LAMS `ora-skill-store-drift-check` (weekly Monday 12:10 PM ET) has posted nothing to its Notion Ops Hub thread since 2026-07-21, despite the registry showing it fired on schedule since.

**Registry check (read via Read tool, not Bash, per the config-write-guard's own read-vs-write guidance):** task is `enabled: true`, cron `10 12 * * 1` correct, `lastRunAt: 2026-08-03T16:17:56.044Z` — i.e. it DID dispatch on the most recent scheduled Monday (7 min after the 16:10 UTC target, normal jitter). No 07-27 lastRunAt is retained (registry keeps only the latest), so that week's outcome can't be read directly from the registry.

**No execution transcript found for either the 07-27 or 08-03 fire.** The task's `notifySessionId` (`local_4ba522cd-e5b2-447e-9bb0-d07d4186c402`) container session's transcript (`.claude/projects/.../f6eb7694....jsonl`, 632 lines) and `audit.jsonl` (1472 lines) both only span 2026-07-07 through 07-08 — the task's original setup/registration window. Nothing for either recent fire exists in this session's stored artifacts at all: not a completed run, not an error, not a partial attempt.

**Most likely explanation, by mechanism and timing (not independently proven for this specific task):** this is the exact fingerprint of the fleet-wide "phantom dispatch" defect root-caused and fixed 2026-08-05 (see the same-day event_log entries: "ROOT CAUSE: the stuck-session watchdog was killing Claude Desktop's renderer" + the `ora-task-integrity-guard` v1.11 / `automation-health-monitor` v1.19 follow-through). `stuck-session-watchdog.ps1` was misclassifying and killing the desktop app's own Electron renderer/utility/gpu child processes (1,645 kills observed, 155 of them renderers) — a renderer is what the scheduler needs attached to actually execute a dispatch, and the scheduler stamps `lastRunAt` regardless (a stale-clear event stamps it identically to a completed run), so a phantom (never-attached) fire is byte-identical to a successful one in the registry and leaves **no transcript, no exit code, nothing to find** — exactly what's missing here. Renderer-absence was measured deterministic for failure (0 of 53 confirmed) and covered ~59% of observed hours, concentrated in daytime windows; both of this task's misses (07-27, 08-03) predate the 08-05 fix (`e441130`, two new watchdog exclusions), so neither could have benefited from it.

**This mechanism was proven CC/MCP-side** (`ora-task-integrity-guard`'s own 08-04/08-05 misses, with quoted stale-clear log lines); it plausibly extends to LAMS/Cowork fires too since both fleets dispatch through the same Claude Desktop app/renderer, but no LAMS-side phantom-dispatch-probe exists to confirm it directly for this task the way the CC-side probe did for its own guard. Treat this as the leading hypothesis, not a closed finding.

**How to close this out:** the next scheduled fire is tomorrow, 2026-08-10 (Monday 12:10 PM ET) — the first one since the 08-05 fix. If it posts normally, that corroborates phantom-dispatch as the cause retroactively. If it stays silent again, the cause is something else specific to this task (Notion write failure, a step-4 idempotency false-positive, or a genuine content/logic defect) and needs a closer look then — not guessed at now.

No writes made — registry read via Read tool only, transcript/audit files read-only, no edits to the SKILL.md, registry, or Notion.

## 2026-08-05 — EnterWorktree can't reach ~/.claude: root-caused, baseRef gap fixed

**Investigation (L5, Engineering OS):** `EnterWorktree({name})` failed from a normal session with "not in a git repository and no WorktreeCreate hooks are configured." Root cause confirmed: the tool anchors to the *launch directory's* repo — the session launch dir (`OneDrive - Oxford Capital Partners`) isn't a git repo, and `~/.claude` is a sibling, not nested inside it, so the tool has nothing to walk to.

**No clean tool-level fix exists — working as intended.** WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks are real and documented (confirmed in the settings.json schema) but are global: pointing them at `~/.claude` would silently redirect *every* future `EnterWorktree` call from any non-git launch dir (the ORA default) into `~/.claude`, regardless of intent. Left unconfigured. Manual fallback stays `git worktree add ~/.claude/worktrees/<name> -b <branch> <base>` (no `.gitignore` entry needed — fail-closed default-deny covers it).

**Second finding, FIXED:** `worktree.baseRef` was unset in `settings.json`, silently defaulting to `"fresh"` (branches from `origin/<default-branch>`). `~/.claude`'s local `main` routinely runs ahead of unpushed `origin/main` (same pattern as `ora-skills`, `oxford-command-center`) — "fresh" would silently drop that ahead-of-origin work from any new worktree. Gabriel approved (in-turn) setting `worktree.baseRef: "head"` globally; applied via the config-write-guard override-token path, `settings.json` re-validated as parseable JSON post-edit. Detail: [reference_enterworktree_launch_dir_repo_detection.md](reference_enterworktree_launch_dir_repo_detection.md).

No data loss, no corruption, at any point in this chain — every deviation was caught by checking ground truth before acting, not discovered after.

**Pattern worth naming:** this is now the third time in one session that a plan built on a snapshot of shared repo state (HEAD, a claim, a push status) went stale between decision and execution because another concurrently-active session moved it first. The fix each time was re-verifying immediately before acting rather than trusting the snapshot — caught the claim-collision, caught the merge landing mid-operation, caught this one. Worth naming as a standing discipline for any future multi-session-concurrent work on this checkout: verify state fresh at the moment of the destructive/history-affecting action, not at the moment of deciding to take it.

## 2026-08-05 — CORRECTION: commit 57d0acf's message understates its own contents (git commit --only misunderstanding, no data lost)

**What happened.** Attempting the isolated-hunk commit Gabriel asked for on `open-items-tracker.md` (concurrently mid-edit by other live sessions, with a ~636-line appsec-sweep addition — OI-078 through OI-091 — interleaved too close in the file for git to split into separate hunks by default), I built a clean target via `git show HEAD:<path>` + programmatic substitution of exactly my 3 known edits (OI-020 close, OI-025 close, OI-101 file), verified with `git diff --no-index` that only 4 hunks / 33 insertions / 3 deletions resulted, staged that exact blob via `git hash-object -w` + `git update-index --cacheinfo`, and confirmed `git diff --cached --stat` showed the intended small diff.

**Then `git commit --only -F <msg> -- <path>` silently discarded that staged blob.** `--only`/`-o` does not commit "whatever is currently staged for this path" — per git's actual semantics, it takes the CURRENT WORKING TREE content for the given pathspec (equivalent to a fresh `git add <path>` at commit time), overriding whatever custom blob was in the index. My careful isolation was bypassed entirely; the commit captured the full working-tree state — everyone's concurrent edits, not just mine.

**Verified impact, immediately:**
- `git status --porcelain` for the file is now EMPTY (working tree = new HEAD) — confirms the commit absorbed all pending edits from other sessions, not just mine.
- New HEAD contains OI-078 through OI-097: the full appsec-sweep findings (6 CRITICAL/HIGH Supabase RLS + auth findings on ora-pm, plus oxford-command-center findings) and the workbook debt-service items (OI-092-097), none of which I wrote or reviewed.
- **No data loss, no corruption.** The committed content is byte-identical to the authentic working-tree file that existed a moment before — it's real, legitimate work from other sessions, just mis-attributed under a commit message describing only my 3 items.
- **Not pushed.** `57d0acf` sits 1 commit ahead of `origin/main`, local only.
- Working tree on disk was never touched by any of my plumbing commands (only the git index/HEAD were manipulated) — no other session's in-progress Edit/Read state was disrupted; a future Edit against unchanged content still works normally for them.

**Deliberately NOT fixed via `git commit --amend`** — CLAUDE.md's git safety protocol is explicit and unconditional: always create new commits, never amend, unless Gabriel explicitly requests it. This entry is the correction of record instead. If Gabriel wants the commit message actually rewritten (safe to do — unpushed, no one else has fetched it), that's his call to make explicitly, not mine to do unprompted.

**Lesson, for next time this technique is needed:** `git commit --only <pathspec>` is NOT the isolation primitive it looks like — it re-reads the working tree. The correct way to commit a custom-staged blob without pathspec interference is a BARE `git commit -F <msg>` with **no pathspec argument at all**, once the index has been prepared via `update-index` and verified clean elsewhere (`git diff --cached --stat` covering the WHOLE repo, not just the one path, showing only the intended file). Today's earlier successful isolated commits (`8a4d51d`, `2f4f831`, `13448b9`, `f9c1c34`, `462d4f1`) all used plain `git add -- <specific files>` on files with NO concurrent interleaved edits from other sessions, so this particular failure mode never triggered for them — this is the first time this session hit a file with edits too close together for git's own hunk-splitting, and the first time the `--only` pathspec trap applied.

- SECOND ERROR: "three files hold plaintext tokens" came from a grep matching the variable NAME `NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN`, not assigned values. SHA-256 digest comparison (no value ever printed) shows only ONE file holds an actual token value — `oxford-realty_archived-20260726/oxfordra-net/.claude/settings.json` — it is a single credential consistent with the already-revoked PAT, and the other two files are name-only mentions.
- NET: one dead credential string in one archived file. Housekeeping, not security.
- Runbook v02 issued superseding v01, stating plainly that v01 was wrong.
- LESSON: a tracker's summary row is not its status. Open the detail block before escalating. The Open table is the surface a reader hits first, so a stale row there does not merely lose work — it MANUFACTURES URGENCY.
- Another session had already filed this exact defect class today as OI-098 ("CLOSED detail, row still in the Open table: OI-029, OI-047, OI-076"). Appended OI-020 and OI-025 to that inventory plus a note that the class caused a real false alarm — argues for a severity bump.

**PLAN-GATE IN-TURN RESET SHIPPED** (`f9c1c34`). Telemetry: 209/644 = **32.5%** override rate (the 41% in memory was 3 weeks stale). Dominant reason class is verbatim "the user already approved this in-turn". eos-plan-gate CANNOT see prompts (payload carries only session_id + tool_input), so detection lives in `engineering-router.py` (UserPromptSubmit).
- DESIGN: a qualifying directive RESETS the edit budget rather than writing a permanent override. A permanent bypass disables the gate for the whole session after one qualifying prompt, so later unplanned sprawl goes uncaught; a reset gives a fresh budget per scoped instruction, so sprawl WITHIN a directive is still caught. Resets log to `plan-gate-resets.log` so telemetry can distinguish auto from human and the measured rate stays honest.
- Detection deliberately conservative — imperative AND a concrete scope signal (numeric range, >=2 explicit "item N" refs, plan/list reference, or >=3 enumerated lines). Differential battery **21/21 incl. 12 negative controls**: "fix this", "Proceed", "3 monitors and 2 keyboards", "summarize the last 3 commits", "explain step 1 and step 2" all correctly do NOT reset. False positives silently weaken a gate; false negatives cost one manual override (status quo).

**COMMIT-PROVENANCE COMPOUND-ADD BYPASS — REFUTED, not fixed.** `git_commit_parse.candidate_paths()` ends with `cands |= pending_add_paths(repo, cmd)` under a comment naming this exact case. Three confirmations: unit probe (file SEEN in `add -A &&`, `add . &&`, `add -A ;` while unstaged); **existing tests already covered it** (test-commit-provenance-guard.py:1031/1046/1119, green) — the 2026-07-24 speculation was never checked against the suite that already disproved it; and `commit -a` semantics verified to match git's real behavior. The ORIGINAL observation (a janitor commit that should have blocked) stays unexplained — only this explanation is dead; the untested `except Exception: pass` path is now the leading candidate.

## 2026-08-05 — ROOT CAUSE: the stuck-session watchdog was killing Claude Desktop's renderer (Code session)

Follow-on to the same-day phantom-dispatch forensics. Gabriel asked how to fix the ~45% phantom rate; the answer turned out to be self-inflicted. **ORA's own `stuck-session-watchdog.ps1` was killing the desktop app's Electron child processes, including 155 renderers — and a renderer is precisely what the scheduler needs to attach a dispatch.**

**The causal chain, evidenced end to end:**
1. `Get-KillCandidates` excluded only two things: CommandLine ≤200 chars (the bare shell) and `--resume=` (interactive sessions). Electron names its own children `claude.exe`, gives them 851–5016-char command lines, passes no `--resume=`, and keeps them alive for the life of the window — so all of them passed both exclusions into the >90min age test.
2. Cross-referencing `stuck-session-watchdog.log` against the app's own `[process-memory]` PID→role telemetry: **391 `electron_utility`, 155 `electron_renderer`, 88 `electron_gpu`, 4 `electron_main` killed** (1,645 kills total; the other 1,007 were genuine sessions). Most recent renderer kill: 2026-08-05T19:05:04Z, PID 33084 — the same renderer that had served the successful 13:05 dispatch.
3. Renderer presence is effectively deterministic for dispatch success: **renderer present → 74 of 76 confirmed; renderer absent → 0 of 53.** Splitting on network state kills the earlier network hypothesis outright: renderer absent + network fine = 31 stale / 0 confirmed; renderer present + network DOWN = 0 stale / 4 confirmed. **Network was a red herring** — a correlate of sleep/teardown, not a cause.
4. Renderer absent **59% of the observed 114.6h**. The ~2h-spaced daytime dark windows (07:03→11:08, 07:30→09:49, 13:05→14:42, 13:35→14:55, 17:05→18:48) match the watchdog's 30-min/90-min cull cadence.

**⚠️ Correction to this morning's entry:** it called the renderer signature "a predictor, not a proven mechanism," citing confirmed runs at `electron(5)`. That conflated *process count* with *renderer presence* — a 5-process app can still have a renderer. Properly split, it is 0-for-53 / 74-of-76. The mechanism is established, not merely correlated.

**Fixes shipped (`e441130`):**
- `stuck-session-watchdog-lib.ps1`: two new exclusions — `--type=` (Electron child marker; the Claude Code CLI never passes it) and `WindowsApps\Claude_` (packaged desktop app vs the CLI's `…\claude-code\<version>\claude.exe`). Both fail SAFE toward not killing. 6 new tests using command lines copied from the live process table, not invented.
- **REFUTE differential harness** (old vs new filter over the live 25-process table, threshold 0 so the filter alone is measured): **16 spared** (4 renderers, 1 gpu, 11 utility), **0 newly killed** (regression gate), **all 7 real CLI task sessions still reachable**. Verdict PASS.
- `ensure-claude-renderer.ps1` (new, 7 tests): the wake task guarded on `Get-Process Claude`, which is TRUE for a tray-only app with no renderer — the exact state where dispatches die — so it never relaunched during the outages it existed to prevent. Now classifies RENDERER / NO-RENDERER / NOT-RUNNING and restores the window. Windows task `ORA Claude Desktop Wake-and-Launch` action re-pointed at it; **trigger unchanged (daily 04:45)**. Old action recorded in the commit message for rollback.
- Gabriel's rulings this session: fix the filter now (over pause-first / retire); harden Wake-and-Launch (over retiming crons); keep the phantom alert bar at "any phantom" for now — the alert going quiet is how we will know the fix worked.

**Verification:** stuck-session-watchdog 15/15 · ensure-claude-renderer 7/7 · phantom-dispatch-probe 20/20 · Python suite 16/17. The one failure is NOT from this work — `reference_workbook_annual_debt_service_366day_overcapture.md` is untracked, written 15:34 today by a concurrently-working session, and trips `governor-drift-probe` on a `2.641x` DSCR figure in prose. Left alone per single-writer doctrine; it will block whoever pushes next.

**Open / next:**
- **Re-measure the phantom rate in ~48h.** Expect the daytime component to collapse; if it does not, the renderer is dying for a third reason. `_state/phantom-dispatch.log` carries the daily rate line, so the trend is already being recorded.
- Overnight dark windows (19:00→04:45, 22:05→09:30) are the machine asleep / window closed, not the watchdog. The 04:45 daily guard covers the morning edge only. If post-fix data still shows overnight losses, the next lever is raising the guard's frequency — deliberately NOT done today, because a window that pops open every 30 minutes is an intrusion Gabriel did not ask for.
- Still needs Gabriel's explicit approval (both behind `config-write-guard`): wiring the phantom probe into `ora-task-integrity-guard` STEP 1.5, and adding a "check the desktop log before attributing a defect to a SKILL.md" step to `automation-health-monitor`'s triage.
- Nothing pushed. Two commits from the earlier entry (`a4f946b`, `66b562a`) plus `e441130` sit local; the checkout has ~82 files dirty from three other sessions.

**Workflow-optimization candidates:**
- *(doctrine)* A guard that kills processes needs an allow-list of what it may kill, not a deny-list of what it may not. Both of the old exclusions were deny-list heuristics inferred from two observed shapes; the class that broke it (Electron's own children) simply was not among the shapes considered. Worth applying to any other ORA script that terminates, deletes, or archives by pattern.
- *(doctrine)* This bug was invisible for three weeks because its *victim* was the thing that reports health. Any watchdog whose failure mode is "silences the fleet" must be verified against an out-of-band signal — the phantom probe is now that signal for this one.
- *(friction)* The watchdog shipped 2026-07-15 WITH a unit-test suite and the suite passed throughout. The tests encoded the same two-shape assumption as the code, so they could never have caught it. A fixture set derived from the *live* process table (as the 6 new tests now are) would have.

## 2026-08-05 — Automation Health 2026-08-05 follow-up: CC transcript + GitHub items (Code session)

Three items Cowork could not reach from its surface. **Both fleet defects turned out to be ONE root cause — phantom dispatch — and both of Cowork's working hypotheses are refuted.** Evidence: `%APPDATA%\Claude\logs\main1.log` + `main.log` (`[CCDScheduledTasks]` / `[ScheduledTasks]`), the CC session store, `~/.claude/maintenance/_state/`, and Windows Task Scheduler.

1. **ora-task-integrity-guard partial-run pattern (08-04, 08-05) — ROOT-CAUSED. Not a partial run: the task never started on either day. SKILL.md-length hypothesis REFUTED; no split performed.**
   - **The premise was wrong.** `emit-fleet-heartbeat.py`'s output is NOT written by this task. `_state/fleet-heartbeat.json` (mtime 08-05 07:30:11 ET) is written by the **Windows Task Scheduler** job `ORA Fleet Heartbeat Push` (daily 07:30, LastRun 08-05 07:30:01) via `maintenance/push-fleet-heartbeat.ps1` — outside both Claude fleets by design. `push-fleet-heartbeat.log` confirms `emit: ORA FLEET HEARTBEAT written cc=27 lams=27` at `2026-08-04T11:30:02Z`. So "wrote step X but not steps Y/Z" was never a partial run — the guard wrote **nothing** on either day, and a different runner supplied the one artifact that looked alive.
   - **No transcript exists to pull.** The CC session store holds no session titled `Ora task integrity guard` for 08-04 or 08-05; the most recent is 08-03 (createdAt 11:29:30, itself a catch-up). A truncated session would have left a transcript with early steps done — there is none.
   - **What actually happened**, from the desktop log:
     ```
     08-04 07:29:07  Spawning new session ... ora-task-integrity-guard { missed: '2026-08-04T11:05:00.000Z' }
     08-04 07:45:05  [warn] Cleared stale pending dispatch for: ora-task-integrity-guard
     08-05 07:05:22  Delaying dispatch for ora-task-integrity-guard by 559s (jitter)
     08-05 07:14:41  Spawning new session ... ora-task-integrity-guard
     08-05 07:20:22  [warn] Cleared stale pending dispatch for: ora-task-integrity-guard
     ```
     Neither day produced a `Confirmed task run for:` line. This is the phantom-dispatch class already documented in `reference_scheduler_lastrunat_stamped_at_dispatch` (root-caused 08-03 on `ora-health-guard`) — **it was simply never checked for these two tasks.**
   - **`lastRunAt` is stamped by the stale-clear itself.** Registry `lastRunAt` = `2026-08-05T11:20:22.767Z` — matches the 07:20:22 ET stale-clear to the millisecond; the 08-04 value carried in the next day's spawn line was `2026-08-04T11:45:05.316Z` = the 07:45:05 stale-clear. A never-started task is byte-identical to a completed one in the registry.

## 2026-08-04 — ora-pm appsec sweep: OI-063/OI-069/OI-045 closed via 3-round REFUTE cycle; OI-045 escalated MEDIUM→CRITICAL mid-fix

Continuing the appsec sweep, Gabriel asked for a status check on OI-041/042/045/046/048 (previously closed in the tracker on the strength of commit messages, never independently re-verified). A `git log` check on `ora-pm` found merged commits for all five that the tracker still listed as OPEN. Dispatched 5 parallel REFUTE-pass agents (security-auditor) to independently re-verify each against the actual current code, not trust the commit messages.

Results: OI-041 and OI-042 (original scope) were genuinely closed. Three were not: OI-063 (a self-flagged 5-file gap in OI-042's error-hygiene sweep — a commit titled "dbError sweep" hadn't actually touched any of the 5 files), OI-069 (CAM recalculation could silently reopen and under-bill an already-billed reconciliation — a commit titled "OI-046 gap closure" turned out to be an unrelated fix), and OI-045 (MFA/AAL2 step-up was enforced client-side only — the enroll/verify UI flow itself had been fixed earlier, but nothing on the server ever checked whether a session had completed the challenge). Gabriel approved fixing all three under the session's established TDD+REFUTE pattern.

Isolated the three fixes in a shared worktree (`fix/oi-063-069-045-remaining-gaps`):
- **OI-063**: routed all 9 sites across the 5 files through the existing `dbError()` helper. Mechanical, low-risk.
- **OI-069**: a first REFUTE pass on the initial (check-then-act) fix found a genuine TOCTOU race — a concurrent `/:id/approve` could still bill the row in the window between the pre-check and the write. Rewrote as an atomically-conditional update (`.eq('status','draft')` as the concurrency control itself, same idiom OI-046 already used), with an insert-fallback for first-time calculations. A second REFUTE pass then found the guard was a deny-list (`!= 'billed'`) that would have silently reopened a `'collected'` reconciliation too — a third legal status per the DB's own CHECK constraint, currently unreachable but latent. Fixed to an allow-list (`== 'draft'`).
- **OI-045**: built `server/middleware/aal-guard.ts` (`requireAal2`), using Supabase's documented server-side/stateless form of `auth.mfa.getAuthenticatorAssuranceLevel(jwt)` — a real network round-trip, not a locally-decoded claim — mirroring the existing client-side `mfa-guard.ts` decision logic. Wired onto `PATCH /api/portal/autopay`. A second REFUTE pass found that scope was far too narrow: `POST /api/stripe/setup-intent` (attaches the bank account in the first place) and `POST /api/stripe/payment-intent` (confirms and charges immediately — the single most sensitive path, moves real money) were both still completely ungated, independently exploitable of `/autopay`. Escalated the item from MEDIUM to CRITICAL and gated both. A third REFUTE pass swept the rest of `server/routes/` for any other tenant-JWT-reachable financial-write path — none found, confirmed complete. `POST /api/stripe/customer` deliberately left ungated (no PM/money involved); a low-severity unrelated finding surfaced there (unvalidated email/name reaching Stripe) and was filed separately as OI-077 rather than expanding scope.

All three fixes shipped with TDD (RED tests before the fix) and end-to-end integration tests proving the real middleware is wired onto the real routes against the real app — not just unit-testing the middleware in isolation. Merged to `ora-pm` main (commit `a29f8f0`), after first merging in two commits another concurrent session had pushed in the meantime (OI-047's Outlook-COM cron handoff, OI-073/074's migration-tracking root-cause fix) — clean merge, no conflicts, re-verified 448/448 green post-merge before pushing.

OI-071 (the PortalInsurance upload-path bug from OI-067's earlier work) independently corroborated by the OI-048 REFUTE pass — noted, not re-filed. Whole-branch review (dispatched before deploy) caught and fixed three real defects before they shipped: an exit-code capture bug that would have logged every successful send as failed, UTF-8 mojibake corrupting every non-ASCII character in the digest emails (Hono's `c.json()` omits a charset; Windows PowerShell 5.1 mis-decodes), and tenant PII/balances that would have landed in an unrotated plaintext `cron.log`.

Six weeks of missed critical-date alerts and — more materially — missed late-fee posting on overdue tenant balances. Re-registered and confirmed live; the verification runs cleared the real backlog (10 critical-date alerts, 24 delinquent tenants, 7 late fees posted, idempotency-protected against duplicates).

Two tooling gotchas fixed in the same session: `wrangler pages deploy` with no branch override tags the deploy with whatever git branch is locally checked out, not server-side state — a first deploy attempt from the feature-branch worktree silently shipped a preview alias, not `ora-pm.pages.dev` (fixed by redeploying from a `main` checkout; documented in `tech.md` §11 + `reference_ora_pm.md`). `ping-crons.ps1`'s 90s client timeout was too tight for `delinquency-check`'s real backlog-clearing runtime (~93s measured) — bumped to 240s.

## 2026-08-04 — Rollout mistake: shipping OI-id enforcement as BLOCK taxed every other session; downgraded to WARN

Corrects the record on tonight's OI-id allocator work. The mechanics — reservation-based allocation, baseline grandfathering, `--backfill`, the checker's guidance pointing at it — are all sound and independently REFUTE-verified. **The mistake was operational: shipping enforcement in BLOCK mode was premature, and it cost every other session working tonight, not just this one.**

**What happened.** Enforcement landed and immediately blocked the push. The blocker was a real, legitimate item (`OI-070`, fleet-status.py work from another session) filed in the gap between capturing the baseline and enforcement actually going live — a transition-window case, handled correctly via `--backfill`. Then it happened again nineteen minutes later with `OI-071` (ora-pm COI upload path, also legitimate, also another session's work). **Two collisions caught in one hour, and zero of them were real collisions.** Both were ordinary filing by sessions that had no way to know an allocator existed, because it had shipped minutes earlier and nothing told them to use it.

**The asymmetry, stated as the actual design criterion, not just a retrospective excuse.** A missed collision costs one renumber, and `check-open-items-duplicate-ids.py` has caught every real one for weeks — `OI-027`, `OI-061`, `OI-066`. A wrongly-blocked push stalls **every concurrent session** until a human manually intervenes. Shipping BLOCK before adoption existed inverted that trade: instead of removing a rare cost, it introduced a frequent one and handed the bill to whoever pushed next, for a defect they did not cause. That is the finding worth keeping, independent of this specific tool: **a blocking check for an unadopted workflow is not enforcement, it is a tax.**

**Fix, not a revert.** `_state/oi-id-enforcement-mode.txt` (`WARN`/`BLOCK`, default `WARN`, fails toward `WARN` on an unreadable file — same "gate must not spontaneously start blocking on its own config failure" principle as the baseline's fail-open). WARN still surfaces the violation and the remedy in the pre-push output; it just doesn't fail the push. Tested explicitly in both directions: WARN exits 0 while still naming the ID and `--backfill`, and BLOCK still exits 1, so WARN did not quietly disarm the check. The flip criterion is written into the mode file itself: switch to BLOCK once the reservation ledger shows allocations from sessions **other than** the one that built this — not "once the tracker looks clean," since clean today only means nobody filed today.

**Advertised** in `session-context.md`, the file every session auto-loads at start — the piece that was actually missing and the root cause of both incidents. One process note: my first draft of that bullet ran 87 words against the file's own 80-word-per-bullet doctrine cap, and the probe caught it. Trimmed to 44; the reasoning lives in the mode file and here, not in the pointer. `session-context.md` is gitignored, so the advert itself is local-only to this machine — acceptable, since its purpose is guiding sessions running here, and the durable record of *why* is this entry plus the tracked mode file.

**Scoreboard, for the honest version of tonight's ship:** 18 enforcement tests (was 10), all green; adversarial REFUTE held in both the must-not-block and must-block directions before this correction, and nothing here weakens either — WARN and BLOCK are now both independently tested. Two real collisions caught, zero false blocks going forward pending adoption.

## 2026-08-04 — Atomic OI-id allocator shipped: the structural fix for the ID-collision pattern, plus checker wiring

The companion to the same-day entry recording that the concurrent-session collision pattern **recurred twice in one session** — that one documents the pattern; this one closes it. `check-open-items-duplicate-ids.py` has been the standing CATCH since OI-027 (2026-07-27) and it works: it caught OI-061 and OI-066 within one hour on 08-03/04. But it catches *after* the fact, and because it runs in the pre-push hook-tests gate, **one session's collision blocks every session's push** until somebody renumbers. Three of tonight's pushes were blocked by collisions that were not the pusher's work.

**The design insight, and why the obvious fix fails.** "Read the tracker's highest OI-NNN, add one" is not wrong because reading is slow. It is wrong because **minutes pass between reading the max and committing the row**, and throughout that window the tracker still shows the OLD max. A second session reading in good faith gets the same answer — both were correct at the instant they looked. A counter therefore does not fix this either; nothing that only consults current state can, because the problem is a gap in time, not a stale read. Same decay this session already recorded in [[feedback_findings_decay_recheck_before_writing]].

So allocation records a **durable reservation at hand-out time**, and every later allocation takes `max(highest in tracker, highest reserved) + 1`. An id is burned the moment it is issued, whether or not the row is ever written — deliberate: ids are free, collisions are not. Unwritten reservations surface in `--report` as ORPHANED and are **never auto-reclaimed**, because reclaiming is precisely how the window reopens.

**Correctness details that carry the weight.** Serialisation is an `O_EXCL` lock (atomic on Windows and POSIX). A crashed holder cannot wedge it: locks older than `stale_lock_secs` are broken **and reported on stderr** rather than silently. `fsync` before the lock drops, so a kill between append and release cannot lose an id already handed out. It **refuses** when the tracker is unreadable — that path would return OI-001 and collide with everything, and a loud failure beats a confidently wrong id. The id regexes are copied verbatim from the checker so the two can never disagree about what counts as taken; section-only ids count, since a detail section with no row yet is somebody's in-flight item.

**Testing.** TDD, 12 tests written red first. The load-bearing ones are concurrency: 12 racing **threads** and 8 racing **processes** — threads alone would not prove it, because real sessions are separate processes and a thread-only test would pass against a lock that doesn't survive process boundaries. Adversarial REFUTE, **NOT REFUTED**: 24-process race (unique, contiguous, no leaked lock); an exception inside the critical section leaks nothing and the allocator recovers; ledger stays well-formed at 16/16 unique under load; a **fresh** lock is respected — it waits, then refuses, rather than stealing; live dry-run against the real tracker read 68 ids at the time.

**Wiring (`591813e`), which mattered more than it looks.** The check caught the collision and then sent the reader straight back to the procedure that causes it — "renumber the newer one" is correct and useless alone, because the only obvious way to pick a replacement is max+1. The guidance now names the allocator **and states the mechanism**: the tracker shows the old max for the whole minutes-long gap. Stating the why was the deliberate choice — someone who understands the window will not work around the tool, whereas a bare command invites "I'll just add one this once." Verified the recommended invocation is copy-pasteable rather than aspirational (ran it against the real tracker with a temp ledger: returned OI-070, real ledger untouched at 0 reservations). Two assertions pin the pointer and the max+1 warning so a later edit cannot silently drop them and leave the check dispensing advice that reproduces the defect. 31/31, was 29/29.

**Scope, stated honestly: discoverable, NOT enforced.** Nothing stops a session hand-assigning an id, and the pointer only appears once a collision has already been caught. Enforcement — gating hand-assigned ids at commit time — is a real design decision with genuine false-positive risk (legitimate hand-edits, backfills, merge resolutions) and was deliberately left undone rather than bolted on.

**Scale of the churn this addresses:** the tracker went from 62 to 69 rows in roughly two hours, with two id collisions in that window, both self-resolving before anyone renumbered. Gate now runs 65 test files (was 63) — the 12 allocator tests plus another session's new `test-gitfixture.py`, which landed the OI-061 shared-fixture refactor while this was in flight. Commits: `9d9dd27` allocator, `591813e` checker wiring, both on `origin/main`.

Gabriel chose doc + surface-check over attempting environment-aware `CACHE_ROOT` resolution (flagged as likely infeasible — the Read tool reaches the cache via host access, not this sandbox's mount namespace) or parking it unaddressed. ## 2026-08-03 — Concurrent-session collision pattern recurred twice in one session (ora-skills, then ~/.claude), same underlying gap: the claim mechanism exists but isn't used for routine git writes

Two fresh instances of the recurring [[reference_concurrent_session_duplicate_hardening_work]] pattern, ~40 minutes apart, in the same session:

**1. `ora-skills`.** Asked to reconcile a diverged `main` (local 3 commits vs `origin/main` 3 commits). Resolved the genuine conflict in `tools/pending_reimport.py` (verified local's version a strict superset of origin's), then watched `HEAD` advance to a merge commit (`a22410a`) and land on the GitHub remote without this session ever running `git add`/`git commit`/`git push`. Content was correct (39/39 tests, re-verified independently) — a concurrent session running the identical reconciliation on the same non-worktree-isolated checkout finished first. `hooks/active-work/repo-housekeeping.json` showed session `83715320-ea98-4ae2-8ebd-e3ec6f2163dd` claimed `repo-housekeeping` at `2026-08-03T21:44:29`, 4 minutes after this session's own merge commit landed (`21:40:51` per reflog) — real evidence of concurrent activity in the window, though that specific claim (PR #35 branch cleanup) doesn't itself explain the push. Full detail already logged same day: "ora-skills merge-push attribution."

**2. `~/.claude` itself.** Committing the resulting event_log entry surfaced two more races: another session had already committed it (`38e9f9c`, bundled with unrelated pending entries — benign, `event_log.md` has no single-writer rule by design, see [[reference_event_log_uncommitted_backlog]]); then pushing to the private backup remote (`ZeOoba/ora-claude-config`) produced an auto-merge (`7ef3e65`) absorbing an unrelated PR #36 pushed by a different concurrent session, and after the push completed, `origin/main` had gained yet another commit (`723040e`, PR #38 log entry) from a third session — all landing cleanly, zero content loss (`event_log.md` verified byte-identical across the merge).

**Pattern-level finding, not just a repeat:** the 2026-07-25/26 recurrences in [[reference_concurrent_session_duplicate_hardening_work]] concluded the gap was "no general-purpose claim slug for ad-hoc repo housekeeping" and shipped one (`repo-housekeeping` — confirmed live, it's the exact slug session `83715320` used above). The slug exists and gets used for *deliberately-scoped* housekeeping sweeps. It does not get used for a plain `git merge`/`git push` — neither this session nor the other session(s) racing it claimed anything before touching `ora-skills` or `~/.claude`. The gap has moved from missing tooling to missing habit.

**Separate, non-collision lesson from the same incident:** don't mistake a slow pre-push hook chain for a credential/network hang. `~/.claude`'s `pre-push` runs a doctrine probe, a 63-test hook-test suite (measured 3m16s alone), and a confidentiality scan in sequence before the network push starts. Three early push attempts here timed out on that chain, not on auth — running the push in the background without an artificial timeout resolved it cleanly.

Full pattern history and today's two paragraphs added to [[reference_concurrent_session_duplicate_hardening_work]] (edit applied on disk; NOT yet committed — `~/.claude` currently has 44 uncommitted files with recorded WIP from two other active sessions, `e7994827` and `ebb67ffe`; committing that edit needs the isolated-hunk technique from [[reference_event_log_uncommitted_backlog]], deferred rather than done blind).

## 2026-08-03 — ora-skills merge-push attribution: unclaimed concurrent-session collision, not a rogue automated push

Follow-up to the same-day entry above ("Skill-install verification found a MAX_PATH false positive..."), which left one thing unresolved: *"finally pushed by a concurrent session"* — unattributed.

Content re-verified independently: `git diff e7ff782 HEAD -- tools/pending_reimport.py` empty (exact match to the intended superset resolution), no leftover conflict markers repo-wide, `python -m unittest tools.test_pending_reimport` 39/39 green.

**Attribution found:** `~/.claude/hooks/active-work/repo-housekeeping.json` shows session `83715320-ea98-4ae2-8ebd-e3ec6f2163dd` claimed `repo-housekeeping` ("clean up squash-merged verb-separators: worktree + local branch (-D) + remote branch, PR 35 merged") at `2026-08-03T21:44:29` — 4 minutes after this session's own merge commit landed (`main@{2026-08-03 21:40:51}` per reflog). That claim is real evidence of concurrent ora-skills activity in the same window, though its stated scope (PR #35 branch cleanup) doesn't itself explain a push to `main`. Combined with the prior entry's identical, independently-arrived-at resolution, the far more likely mechanism is a **third session running this same reconciliation task**, whose `merge`→`commit`→`push` sequence landed on the shared, non-worktree-isolated checkout (`C:\Users\Owner\ora-skills`) while this session's own merge was still mid-conflict on the same files — two processes racing on one working tree, not a rogue automated push. No git hook (native or Claude-harness) references `git push` in a way that would explain an autonomous push; ruled out via `git grep`/hook-config audit before concluding this.

**No content-safety issue** — verified twice now, independently, by two sessions with no coordination. **Real gap:** neither this session nor (apparently) the other(s) ran the mandatory `claim_work.py claim` pre-flight before touching `ora-skills` git state. The single-writer claim protocol exists for exactly this collision and wasn't used by anyone in this window. Going forward: treat the claim as mandatory before ANY git write in `ora-skills`, including a plain `git merge` — not just SKILL.md edits.

## 2026-08-03 — Skill-install verification found a MAX_PATH false positive in the drift detector; third duplicate-work near-miss caught by the claim system

Asked to verify another session's claim that two skills were installed. The claim was half right, and checking it surfaced an unrelated infrastructure defect.

**Install claims, checked against the oracle order rather than the ledger.** `lease-form-qc` — **verified**, both bundled files present and byte-identical to the repo. `masterlease-jurisdiction-rebase` — **overstated**. It is installed, but cache and repo held *different* v1.1.2 text: same version number, different document. The cached copy was a Cowork-surface hand-edit applied straight to the packaged `.skill`, and its own changelog said so — *"Applied directly to the packaged `.skill` in Cowork ahead of the Code-surface source; reconcile SKILL.md on next Code session sync."* That reconcile had never happened. A repo-first violation of the same class as PR #25's earlier recovery, not simple staleness.

**The real find: `skill_drifted()` reports a permanent false positive above Windows MAX_PATH.** `tools/pending_reimport.py` does `if not cache_file.is_file(): return True`. On Windows, `Path.is_file()` returns **False** for any path ≥260 chars unless the `\\?\` prefix is used — the file is present and readable, the stdlib simply cannot see it. Measured on `masterlease-jurisdiction-rebase`'s bundled fixture: **265 chars**, `os.path.exists` False, long-path form True, and the file **byte-identical to the repo**. So the skill was reported drifted forever, and no amount of reinstalling could clear it, because every sweep failed the same way.

Surveyed all 96 bundled cache paths: **1 over the limit, 0 in the 240–260 band**, longest-under being 221. Narrow today — but `CACHE_ROOT` alone consumes 148 characters before any skill name, so the headroom is thin for everything.

**How it was found is the transferable part.** Not by reading the code — by my own checker hitting the *same* false negative and reporting a file as absent that `ls` could plainly see. I distrusted my own output rather than the filesystem. Any ad-hoc drift script written against stdlib path calls silently inherits this and reports phantom missing files; the earlier `ABSENT in cache` line in this session's own output was wrong for exactly that reason and should not be cited as evidence.

**Third duplicate-work near-miss today, and the third time the claim system paid for itself.** Before writing the fix I found session `f2e2a6e5` had claimed it under `repo-housekeeping` **12 minutes earlier**, with an uncommitted `import os` already in the file — mid-edit on the exact function. Gabriel ruled: hand over findings, let them finish. Written to `handoffs/2026-08-03_maxpath-drift-false-positive_findings.md` (that path is chip-claim-locked; claim opened and closed). **No code touched.** They landed `cbffee5` (the fix) and `9ca7e09` (the masterlease reconcile) within the hour.

**Their fix independently verified against the reproduction that found the defect:** the 265-char fixture now resolves, hashes, and compares equal; `skill_drifted()`'s remaining verdict on that skill is driven solely by `SKILL.md`, which is correct and unrelated. Their suite 39/39. Worth recording that the buggy skill was never a clean fixture for its own bug — a test asserting "masterlease disappears from candidates" would fail for the unrelated SKILL.md reason, which is why the handoff recommended a synthetic deep path instead.

**One residual, documented not fixed (`e7ff782`).** `_win_long()` prepends the prefix verbatim, which is right for drive-letter paths and wrong for UNC: `\\srv\share\f` becomes `\\?\\\srv\share\f` (measured), which Windows will not resolve — the file then reads as MISSING, reintroducing the exact false verdict the helper exists to prevent, in a form harder to spot because the path still looks plausible. Latent only: `CACHE_ROOT` is a drive path and the repo side is local. Documented rather than fixed because there is no way to exercise a UNC branch here, and an untested branch is worse than a stated gap. Every long-path helper routes through that one function, so the note names it as the single point of repair.

**The merge was messier than the work.** The same MAX_PATH fix reached the repo **twice** — `cbffee5` committed locally and `21e8795` via PR #37 — so both sides introduced `_win_long` at the same place and collided. Resolved by taking this session's side, but only after proving it safe: a full diff showed the **sole** difference was the 16-line UNC note, implementations otherwise byte-identical, making it a strict superset; then the staged blob hash was checked equal to HEAD's (`1a91d0c`) rather than trusting `--ours` to mean what was intended. Final state `a22410a`, on `origin/main`, all three commits confirmed present, suite green.

**Two process lessons, both cheap to repeat and expensive to miss.**
1. **An aborted merge and a completed merge look identical if you only check `MERGE_HEAD`.** A wait-loop keyed on "merge no longer in progress" fired in 0 s on an *abort*; only HEAD failing to advance to a merge commit revealed it. Wait conditions must assert the goal state, not the absence of the intermediate one.
2. **`git merge … | tail` reports `tail`'s exit code, not git's.** It printed `MERGE EXIT: 0` while git had actually failed with "unmerged files". Same exit-masking trap as the earlier `| tail -20` incident this session — piping any gate and reading `$?` is reading the wrong process.

Throughout, the repo moved repeatedly under the work — behind 1 → behind 3, merge open → aborted → reopened, finally pushed by a concurrent session. Every verdict here came from re-reading state immediately before acting rather than carrying forward the previous observation.

## 2026-08-03 — Override-record em dash: root-caused to a stdin decode, fixed at both levels, 7 historical headings repaired

Seven `event_log.md` headings carried `â€”` where an em dash belongs — every one of them a pre-push override record. The templates were never wrong; **the corruption happened in transit.**

**Root cause.** `log_override_use()` in both gates piped `entry.encode("utf-8")` to `append-event-log.py`'s **stdin**, and that script's stdin branch was a bare `sys.stdin.read()`, which decodes with the Windows locale (cp1252). The em dash's three UTF-8 bytes `E2 80 94` arrived as three cp1252 characters and were re-encoded as `C3 A2 E2 82 AC E2 80 9D`. The `--entry-file` branch always opened with an explicit `encoding="utf-8"`; only stdin did not. This is precisely the hazard [feedback_append_event_log_stdin_encoding.md](feedback_append_event_log_stdin_encoding.md) already prescribed `--entry-file` for — the memory existed and the call site predated or ignored it.

**Why it went unnoticed for weeks:** a mangled heading also defeats any same-heading check, so these records could accumulate without ever colliding. The corruption was self-concealing.

**Fixed at both levels rather than one.** Both gates now write to a temp file and pass `--entry-file`, unlinking in a `finally`. Separately, `append-event-log.py`'s stdin branch now decodes `sys.stdin.buffer` as UTF-8 explicitly, falling back to the old behaviour on `AttributeError`/`UnicodeDecodeError`. Either fix alone closes this; together, a future caller that reaches for stdin is covered too. Merged as `07bd20d`.

**The test would have been worthless written the obvious way.** Asserting on `build_override_entry()`'s output cannot catch this — the template is correct. The new test drives the real `append-event-log.py` end to end. It also **pops `PYTHONIOENCODING` for the duration**: with that set in the ambient environment the child inherits it, the broken stdin path passes, and the test proves nothing. That was not hypothetical — the first run of this test passed green against unfixed code for exactly that reason, and only failed once the variable was stripped. Verified red first (77/79, both encoding assertions failing), green after (79/79), and green with *and* without ambient `PYTHONIOENCODING`.

**Adversarial REFUTE, byte-level not string-level**, both gates, `PYTHONIOENCODING` stripped: `E2 80 94` present, the double-encoded sequence absent, zero temp files leaked. Swept for other stdin callers of `append-event-log.py` — none. **NOT REFUTED.** Regressions clean: doctrine gate suite PASS, `maintenance/_tests/test_git_prepush_doctrine_gate.py` ALL PASS, `test-append-event-log.py` PASS.

**Historical repair (`1776b39`), separate commit by design** — stopping the bleeding and rewriting the past are different decisions. All 7 occurrences were in `## ` headings (07-25 ×1, 07-27 ×5, 08-03 ×1); zero in body text, and no other mojibake class present (checked the U+201C, U+2122 and U+00C2 forms). Verified before writing: substitution count equals occurrence count so nothing outside headings moved; entry count unchanged; each heading differs from its original by the substitution alone; and the concatenation of every non-heading line is byte-identical before and after.

**The five 07-27 records are still five separate entries.** They shared a heading before the repair and share a corrected one after; their *bodies* differ, which is what makes them distinct override events. Nothing about the repair touches that — and it is worth restating because these were nearly deleted as duplicates earlier the same day.

**Concurrency.** A concurrent session held an uncommitted "Save-skill installs confirmed" entry in the working tree throughout, so the repair was staged via the isolated-hunk technique against HEAD and committed with no pathspec; their entry was left untouched. Work was claimed under `hooks-override-auth` with `--paths` cover for both gate files, done in a worktree (blast radius), and the claim released on completion.

## 2026-08-03 — Reimport queue was 8, not 5: `list` is blind to sweep-only drift, and a hash match does not mean installed

Built a Cowork install prompt for the pending skill batch. Two verification errors surfaced on the way, both of which would have shipped a wrong result, and both of which are the *documented* failure modes of the tooling rather than novel bugs.

**1. The queue was undercounted because the wrong command was used.** `_staging/PENDING_REIMPORT.md` listed **5** pending skills, and that number was reported to Gabriel. The authoritative contract is `python tools/pending_reimport.py candidates` — ledger **UNION** a full repo-vs-cache SHA256 sweep — which reports **8**. The three extras (`acquisition-underwriting`, `market-monitor`, `solar-lease-underwriting`) carry **no ledger entry at all**; they exist only in the sweep, meaning their drift either predates the post-commit hook or a hook run failed or was bypassed. This is precisely the retroactive-blindness case `pending_reimport.py`'s own docstring describes when it says `candidates` is "the new consumption contract: the UNION of ledger entries and a fresh sweep, never 'ledger OR derive'." Reading the ledger file directly is equivalent to `list`, and `list` is blind by construction. **Building the batch for 5 would have knowingly left 3 skills stale.**

**2. A hash match is not evidence of installation — confirmed live.** Asked whether the earlier batch had been saved, the naive check said yes for two of three: `tenant-email` and `document-assembly` both hashed **identical to the repo**. Neither had been installed. The post-commit hook copies changed SKILL.mds straight into the runtime cache (it announced this at commit time: *"tenant-email: synced 1 file(s)"*), so the cache can match the repo perfectly with no Save-skill click ever having happened. `main.log` showed no corresponding SkillsPlugin sync. The asymmetry that makes the log authoritative: **the hook's file copy produces no SkillsPlugin log activity, so a non-zero `Delta:` cannot be manufactured by the tooling, whereas a hash match trivially can.** The same hook also explained the third case — `ratify-hurdle-rate` had **no cache directory at all** ("no local AppData mirror installed yet — nothing to sync"), because the hook can only refresh a mirror that already exists. It has never been installed.

`main.log` did show real installs today — deltas of 1 at 16:06, 1 at 16:20, 4 at 16:50, 3 at 17:23 — but cache mtimes place all of them on other skills (`lease-form-qc` 17:05, `xlsx`/`docx`/`pptx` 17:23, `acquisition-underwriting`/`market-monitor`/`solar-lease-underwriting` 16:59). A different workstream, not this batch.

**Batch built.** All 8 packaged to `_staging/2026-08-03_reimport-batch-8/` off HEAD `ea9dddf`, each verified byte-identical to its committed repo files with no `__pycache__`/`.pyc` bundled (the exclusion added to `package_skills.is_bundled()` earlier today). Four are **multi-file and therefore Save-skill-only** — `masterlease-jurisdiction-rebase` (6 files), `acquisition-underwriting`, `lease-form-qc`, `market-monitor` (2 each); the Settings → Capabilities path silently drops subfolder files (reproduced twice 2026-07-11) and a partial install there looks successful.

**Packaging gotcha worth recording:** the first verification pass crashed on `acquisition-underwriting/target-markets.json` — `FileNotFoundError`. That file does not exist at that path. `target-markets.json` is a **repo-root shared dependency** that the packager bundles *into* consuming skills under the skill's own prefix (`SHARED_ROOT_DEPS`). Any verifier that walks `.skill` entries and maps them 1:1 back to repo paths will break on every shared-dep consumer; it must fall back to the repo root by basename.

**Prompt regenerated** at `_staging/2026-08-03_reimport-batch-8/COWORK-PROMPT.md`, hardened with what went wrong here rather than generic instructions: a **pre-click baseline capture** (mtime proves nothing without one), an explicit warning that a hash match does not mean installed with today's case cited, the ranked oracle order (`main.log` delta → mtime-vs-baseline → hash), a requirement to verify **every** bundled file for the multi-file skills, and a closing `candidates` run that must report zero. It also instructs Cowork to **stop and report, never repackage**, if a hash stops matching — `masterlease-jurisdiction-rebase` moved through three commits in one hour (`863a0b3` → `ea9dddf`), so repackaging mid-edit could install someone's half-finished work.

**Standing lesson.** Both errors share a shape: a cheap signal that is *correlated* with the truth was used in place of the signal that *is* the truth. The ledger correlates with the queue; the hash correlates with installation. Neither is the thing itself. Where a tool documents a specific consumption contract (`candidates`, not `list`) or a specific oracle (`main.log`, not the mirror), the documented one is load-bearing and the convenient one will eventually be wrong in the direction that looks fine.

**Still open:** all 8 remain uninstalled — 8 manual Save-skill clicks, which nothing in this flow automates.

## 2026-08-03 — PR #34 merged (skill capture); YAML scalar quoting fixed as a CLASS, not an instance ([PR #35](https://github.com/ZeOoba/ora-skills/pull/35))

[PR #34](https://github.com/ZeOoba/ora-skills/pull/34) merged (`51a1c9a`); canonical checkout fast-forwarded (again — a GitHub merge never updates it, and the scheduled task runs from that checkout).

**The YAML quoting fix is a class fix, and the provenance is why.** `acquisition-underwriting` reported MANUAL-MERGE every run on repo `name: "acquisition-underwriting"` vs cache `name: acquisition-underwriting` — identical YAML meaning. Fixing only the file would have guaranteed recurrence: the QUOTED form in the repo was itself pulled FROM the cache by the 2026-07-27 REPO-FIRST recovery (`20a936e`, byte-exact copy), and the same cache served it UNQUOTED on 2026-08-03. **The platform re-serializes frontmatter on install and its quoting style varies over time.** Three more skills (`lease-form-qc`, `market-monitor`, `solar-lease-underwriting`) sat quoted on BOTH sides and would flip identically on the next style change.

Fix: `_normalize_frontmatter` provides a COMPARE-ONLY view with scalar quoting stripped from top-level keys; `_split_parts` routes working-tree files AND historical git blobs through it so ancestry hashes share the space. Narrow by design — no YAML parser, top-level `key: value` only; block-scalar indicators carry no quotes and their indented continuations aren't top-level keys. Plus repo consistency: `name:` unquoted in all 4 (repo was 4 quoted vs 53 unquoted; names are plain identifiers).

**⚠️ Bug the replayed real-data fixture caught — worth generalizing.** The first cut fed the normalized frontmatter into the REPORTING path too. **Unquoting a YAML scalar discards the leading/trailing whitespace that quotes exist to protect**, so parcel-data-recovery's replayed 203-char truncation reported 202. A compare-only normalization must never reach a reported figure; `description_of`/`version_token_of` now read RAW frontmatter, pinned by a hermetic trailing-space test. The real-data suite from PR #32 earned its keep — no synthetic fixture would have found this.

**Post-commit hook, second observation:** unlike the capture commit (a no-op), this one genuinely CHANGED live cache content for 3 skills whose caches were quoted. Verified after: all 4 caches byte-identical to repo, bodies unchanged, descriptions intact (997/972/901/841 chars). Its 4 PENDING_REIMPORT entries were false again — `sweep_drift` clean, cleared. **Standing pattern: any commit touching a SKILL.md writes the live cache and leaves false ledger entries; verify content and clear in the same session.**

Verified: live drift **47 IN-SYNC / 10 NOT-INSTALLED — zero drifted, zero cache-only, standing MANUAL-MERGE gone**. Full suite green (170 tests, 6 files). PR #35 open.

This session's edit — a second exemption marker plus a general inline opt-out — was **backed out uncommitted** rather than raced, leaving the claim holder to land it. This is the failure mode `reference_concurrent_session_duplicate_hardening_work.md` records from a prior incident; the claim broadcast worked as designed and cost only the wasted edit. **Residual (b) is therefore still open and owned by `bd37c567`, not by this session** — the live probe will keep warning on `document-assembly/SKILL.md:181` until that lands.

Every hit and miss re-judged by eye: 0 false positives, 0 false negatives. Live sweep clean at the time of the local run (VP-ACQUISITIONS across 72 emitters); the pre-push run then surfaced (b), which is why the differential is worth re-running after *every* narrowing rather than once at the end.

Second instance today of a live-emitter class living outside scanner scope (the first: the Zapier OAuth grant, visible only in Netlify's dashboard). **Pattern worth institutionalizing: doctrine probes see repos; outbound reality also lives in %APPDATA%, provider dashboards, and Outlook.**

Reading the line's CONTEXT rather than trusting the probe's match is what separated them. Same lesson as the OI-054 false finding earlier today: a pattern match is a candidate, not a finding.

THREE DEFECTS FOUND BY THE LIVE RUN, all silent rather than erroring:
1. discover_store() takes a store NAME not the 'cc' label -- returned None (same regression task-folder-registration-probe's tests pin).
2. Session metadata uses epoch MILLISECONDS while the registry uses ISO strings, same directory. ISO-only parsing returned None, degrading the lookback to scan-all-history and leaving live-session exclusion never firing -- which produced a FALSE LOST_WRITE against a mid-flight session. New memory: reference_session_store_epoch_vs_registry_iso.md.
3. lastActivityAt stops advancing while a session is BLOCKED on one long tool call; a 20-min liveness window aged out running sessions and consecutive runs disagreed (exit 1 then exit 0). Window now 120 min.

Self-refute pass also tightened the Bash redirect heuristic, which matched '->' and '=>' in read-only commands and would have promoted dangling shell READS into alarms.

SCOPE LIMIT (structural, stated not papered over): CC/MCP only -- LAMS has 154 scheduled-task sessions but ZERO transcripts on disk, so Check A has nothing to read there. A LAMS task can lose a write the same way and this will not see it.

## 2026-08-03 — drift comparator: absent git history no longer degrades into a destructive pull (commit 5b017a6)

Fixes the Critical review finding on the [PR #31](https://github.com/ZeOoba/ora-skills/pull/31) branch. CACHE-AHEAD is **inferred from absence** and is the one direction whose remedy overwrites the authoritative store — so the inference is only sound if the search could have found a match.

`git rev-list HEAD -- <path>` exits 0 with EMPTY stdout for a path with no history; the first cut checked only for `None` (command failure). Two reproduced consequences: an **untracked** SKILL.md reported CACHE-NEWER and prescribed the byte-exact pull; and in a **shallow clone** a section the repo had deliberately DELETED was invisible in the truncated ancestry, so the cache's pre-deletion text read as cache-side-new and the pull would have **re-introduced deleted content** into the repo. The shallow case needed its own guard (`rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`) — the empty-set check does not catch it, because rev-list does return a revision, just not the relevant one. A third guard treats an empty PER-PART ancestor set as UNKNOWN (revisions exist but every blob read failed). Same fix applied to `pending_reimport._file_history_hashes`.

**⚠️ An existing test certified the defect.** `test_file_history_hashes_none_none_when_file_never_committed` was NAMED for `(None, None)` but ASSERTED `set()`, with a comment reasoning that a successful-but-empty `rev-list` "must not be conflated with git-unavailable". That is true at the git layer and wrong at the consumer — `classify_shared_copy` treats any non-`None` set as a completed search. This is why the bug survived into review: the suite was pinning it. Reversed, reasoning recorded in the test, plus an end-to-end assertion that the direction is UNKNOWN not CACHE-AHEAD. Generalizable lesson: **a test whose name and assertions disagree is a defect report, not coverage** — cf. [feedback_fixture_shaped_tests_certify_dead_branches.md](feedback_fixture_shaped_tests_certify_dead_branches.md).

**Residual, undetectable and documented in the docstring:** if the cache content was committed only on a branch later deleted or gc'd, ancestry genuinely no longer holds it, so DIVERGENT decays to CACHE-AHEAD. The safety net therefore **erodes over time** as `clean_gone`/gc prune branches; the MANUAL-MERGE superset gate is the backstop.

Verified: original repro now MANUAL-MERGE/UNKNOWN; a genuine cache superset with full history still CACHE-NEWER (no over-correction); live stores unchanged (neither checkout shallow, all skills tracked, shared-dep reconciliation still 5/5 in sync). [PR #32](https://github.com/ZeOoba/ora-skills/pull/32) rebased onto the new tip; both changesets verified to coexist. Stack green: **153 tests, 6 files**.

## 2026-08-03 — drift comparator: code review + real-data coverage (PR #32), one Critical still open

**Review of [PR #31](https://github.com/ZeOoba/ora-skills/pull/31)** (pr-review-toolkit code-reviewer, opus — reviewer ≥ implementer) returned 1 Critical, 6 Important, 3 Minor, and confirmed the asymmetric superset gate, `split_skill_md` robustness, rename handling, git-missing→UNKNOWN degradation, the read-only contract, and zero import side effects as sound.

**⛔ Critical — RESOLVED same session, commit `5b017a6` on the #31 branch** (status corrected in place; the fix detail is the 2026-08-03 "absent git history" entry above). `skill_drift_report._part_history_hashes` returned an *empty set*, not `None`, when `git rev-list HEAD -- <path>` exits 0 with no output — untracked file, shallow clone, or a `branch -D`'d branch. `classify_shared_copy` then skips the UNKNOWN branch and returns **CACHE-AHEAD**, which can ship the destructive byte-exact pull. Reproduced directly (untracked repo file → verdict CACHE-NEWER; `rev-list` rc=0, stdout=`''`). This is inferred-null masquerading as verified-null inside the very gate meant to enforce that distinction. One-line fix (`ancestors[part] if ancestors and ancestors[part] else None`); the same latent bug exists at `pending_reimport._file_history_hashes`. Notable second-order risk: the DIVERGENT safety net **decays over time** — a cache copy matching a still-live feature branch gives MANUAL-MERGE today and CACHE-NEWER after `clean_gone` or a gc prunes it.

**[PR #32](https://github.com/ZeOoba/ora-skills/pull/32) (stacked on #31) closed both disclosed coverage limits, each hiding a real defect:**
1. **Block-scalar blindness.** `census-acs-extract`, `ratify-hurdle-rate`, `oxford-cc-strategic-audit` declare `description:` as a YAML folded block scalar; the old regex returned literally `'>'`, so `len(cache) < len(repo)` could never fire and **the DESCRIPTION-REGRESSION detector was silently dead on all three**. `description_of` now folds `>`/`|` blocks (incl. chomping indicators), stops at the next top-level key, skips a nested `metadata: description:`, and unquotes quoted scalars — parcel-data-recovery reads **850** chars, matching the incident record, not 852. Conformance sweep added over every real SKILL.md.
2. **Order-blind superset.** `_line_subset` used a `Counter`, so a cache that **reordered AND appended** read as a clean cache-side superset → CACHE-NEWER → byte-exact pull, silently imposing platform section ordering on the authoritative copy. Now an **ordered-subsequence** test. The CACHE-NEWER remedy no longer overstates itself: content + ordering verified, blank-line/whitespace structure explicitly NOT.

The 850→203 truncation is now replayed from the **genuine** 850-char description (real source, real truncation shape — the 203-char string itself was never committed), asserting the named trigger phrases are demonstrably lost. Full suite green: **148 tests, 6 files**.

**Also open (low, reported not absorbed):** `acquisition-underwriting` now yields a recurring MANUAL-MERGE on a YAML **quoting-only** difference — repo `name: "acquisition-underwriting"` vs unquoted in cache. Correct but noisy; cheapest fix is one character in the repo, not a YAML-semantic comparator.

**Live-target premise re-confirmed twice more:** the cache advanced again mid-session (mtime 16:06, after the 15:48 run), and the repo moved under me at rebase — the "41 IN-SYNC / 3 MANUAL-MERGE" figure was only true at repo `189bd28`. Every drift count now carries a revision + read_at stamp.
